problem: Existing VLN agents assume static scenes or treat pedestrians as generic moving obstacles based on implicit visual cues, so they neither semantically recognize task-relevant humans (and bypass them) nor anticipate human motion (and collide).
motivation: Real indoor environments contain dynamic people, and instructions often refer to human activities (e.g. 'stop in front of the two people discussing'). Success requires both semantic understanding of what humans do and geometric foresight of where they move, plus socially compliant distances.
key_idea: A dual-stream human understanding module (pose/trajectory forecasting plus VLM-generated activity descriptions) is fused into the topological map of a waypoint-based VLN agent and regularized with a social distance loss.
insight: Ablations show trajectory features mainly cut collisions (unseen CR 0.48 to 0.41) while pose mainly helps SR (0.20 to 0.22), and the two combine to CR 0.40 / SR 0.23. The VLM adds a further gain (CR 0.40 to 0.36, SR 0.23 to 0.24), and future-oriented features beat past-oriented encodings (SR 0.21 to 0.23). Both social distance loss terms are complementary (unseen CR 0.55 to 0.40 when combined). Gains are small in absolute terms on the SR metric.
method: Human detection and short temporal observation: YOLO-Pose detects humans at each waypoint; the agent pauses to collect 6 frames and forms per-person trajectories

Geometric stream: 17-keypoint pose sequences and depth back-projected 3D positions feed LSTM encoder-decoder predictors that forecast the next 3 frames; the hidden features are used as geometric features, fine-tuned online with pose and trajectory losses
Semantic stream: cropped person views are given to Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct with a navigation-oriented prompt to produce a text description of activity/intent, encoded by a CLIP text encoder

Topological feature fusion: static node features are combined with the mean of geo+sem features over the humans at a node via an MLP, then processed by a cross-modal graph transformer (GASA) plus FFN for waypoint selection (ETPNav/BEVBert-style)

Social Distance Loss: collision penalty (coefficient 3.0) plus a proximity repulsion loss within r_s=1.0 m, with front-facing weighting, added to the pose, trajectory and navigation cross-entropy losses

setting.backbone: ETPNav/BEVBert-style waypoint policy with cross-modal graph transformer (trained), YOLO-Pose, LSTM predictors (fine-tuned), Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct (frozen, zero-shot), CLIP text encoder
setting.model_size: Qwen3-VL-2B for the VLM; total not stated
setting.training_data: Pre-trained in static environments (R2R-CE style, 100k iterations), then fine-tuned online on HA-VLNCE train (10,819 instructions) for 15k iterations
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints on a topological graph (SE(2) relative displacement)

numbers_note: SR and CR are printed as fractions (0-1) in the tables and kept as printed. NE is not reported. Real-world trials: HCSG 41/50 (82%) vs BEVBert 19/50 (38%), 5 scenarios x 10 trials.
results: On HA-VLNCE val-unseen, HCSG reaches CR 0.36 and SR 0.24, versus BEVBert's CR 0.55 and SR 0.21 (the strongest baseline), a 34.5% CR reduction and 14.3% SR gain. On val-unseen BEVBert keeps a better TCR (4.71 vs 5.02). In real-world trials HCSG succeeds in 82% vs 38% for BEVBert.
limitations: Stop-and-wait design: the agent pauses to gather a short observation window rather than streaming continuously
Small absolute SR gains on the benchmark, with a fixed 1.0 m social radius rather than adaptive social distance priors; the real-world evaluation is small (10 trials per scenario in one office)
